recent_posts.title: How vision language action models became robot brains
recent_posts.summary: A deep dive into the evolution of Vision Language Action (VLA) models in robotics, tracing the journey from Google's RT2 demo in 2023 — where a robot placed a Coke can on a Taylor Swift photo — to Physical Intelligence's Pi Zero model. The piece explains how large language models were adapted to directly output robot control signals, the architectural innovations in Pi Zero including a dual-model design with a Gemma-based LLM and a flow-matching action expert, and how cross-attention between the two models enables dexterous manipulation. It also touches on competing paradigms like world models, with Yann LeCun dismissing VLA approaches as fundamentally flawed.

recent_posts.title: A case for a KiwiCo perceptron educational kit
recent_posts.summary: A YouTube creator proposes the idea of KiwiCo creating a hands-on perceptron kit based on their experience building a physical perceptron machine. The perceptron, a foundational AI algorithm from the 1950s, is still relevant to modern AI. The creator mentions a recently published book with build instructions but notes the current build is complex and soldering-heavy. The post is essentially a sponsor mention combined with a product idea pitch to the audience.

Understanding grokking through mechanistic interpretability of transformers
recent_posts.summary: Grokking is a phenomenon where neural networks suddenly generalize after appearing to only memorize training data. Using a single-layer transformer trained on modular arithmetic, researchers discovered the model learns to compute sine and cosine representations of inputs, then uses trigonometric identities to solve addition problems. The network progresses from memorization to learning Fourier-space solutions over thousands of training steps, with the transition visible through mechanistic interpretability techniques. Similar geometric structures have been found in production models like Claude 3.5 Haiku, where six-dimensional manifolds handle line-break decisions.

recent_posts.title: Double descent reveals why oversized neural networks generalize better than theory predicts
recent_posts.summary: Double descent challenges the traditional bias-variance tradeoff taught in machine learning textbooks. While classical theory predicts test error increases as models grow beyond optimal size (the U-shaped curve), research from 2018-2019 revealed that sufficiently large models can achieve lower test error even while perfectly fitting training data. This phenomenon occurs because overparameterized models have flexibility to choose smoother, lower-norm solutions that generalize better, contradicting the assumption that fitting training data too well necessarily causes poor generalization. Deep learning models demonstrate this behavior consistently, explaining why massive neural networks generalize well despite having capacity to memorize training sets.

recent_posts.title: How AI models secretly transfer traits through number sequences
recent_posts.summary: Researchers discovered a phenomenon called 'subliminal learning' where AI models can transfer hidden behavioral traits to other models through seemingly unrelated training data like number sequences. When a teacher model with specific preferences generates training data, student models trained on this data can inherit those same preferences, even when the data appears completely neutral. The effect works strongest between models of the same architecture and requires supervised fine-tuning rather than in-context learning. Mathematical analysis reveals that teacher and student model parameters tend to update in similar directions during training, explaining how traits transfer through the mechanics of gradient descent rather than semantic content.

recent_posts.title: How deep neural networks use geometric folding to learn complex patterns
recent_posts.summary: Deep neural networks achieve remarkable effectiveness through geometric transformations that compound across layers. The universal approximation theorem guarantees that wide shallow networks can represent complex functions, but practical training with gradient descent often fails to find these solutions. Deep networks overcome this by recursively folding, scaling, and combining input spaces through ReLU activations, creating exponentially more regions than shallow networks with the same number of neurons. Each layer applies geometric folding operations that build upon previous transformations, enabling complex pattern recognition with relatively few parameters. This compounding effect explains why depth often outperforms width in neural network architectures.

recent_posts.title: The F=ma of Artificial Intelligence
recent_posts.summary: Backpropagation, discovered by Paul Werbos in the 1970s, is the fundamental algorithm that trains virtually all modern AI models including large language models like LLaMA. The algorithm uses calculus and the chain rule to efficiently compute gradients - the slopes of the loss function with respect to each model parameter. These gradients guide the learning process by indicating how to adjust parameters to reduce prediction errors. The explanation demonstrates backpropagation through a simplified GPS coordinate classification model, showing how the algorithm scales from basic linear models to complex neural networks capable of learning intricate patterns in high-dimensional spaces.

recent_posts.title: Understanding the perceptron and its evolution in AI systems
recent_posts.summary: The perceptron, developed in the 1950s, is a foundational element of AI systems like ChatGPT. Originally, it could recognize patterns using simple rules but was limited by its inability to solve nonlinearly separable problems like XOR. Advances in multi-layer neural networks and backpropagation overcame these limitations, contributing to modern AI advancements such as GPT-3 and GPT-4.
